caption:
Top U.S. officials say the recent wave of tech outages was not a cyberattack.
Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton says systems broke while being patched for newly found vulnerabilities, including at the NSA.
Sen. Mark Warner says AI now finds flaws so fast that everyone patches at once.

Do you buy the patching explanation?

Follow @neurafeed.ai for daily AI news.

Source: ABC News, Fox Business · Photo: NSA
threads_text: U.S. officials say the outages hitting the NSA and other systems were not hackers but rushed security patches. Sen. Warner says AI finds flaws so fast that everyone is patching at once. Do you buy that explanation?

paragraphs.text: Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said on November 17, 2026, that a recent run of U.S. technology outages did not come from a coordinated cyberattack or from state-sponsored activity. Speaking on Fox Business, he said the disruptions came from institutions taking systems down to install security patches after vulnerabilities were identified, and that some of those systems did not come back up as expected.

Clayton tied an outage at the National Security Agency on the same day to that patching work. According to ABC News, an internal communications system that NSA employees use to share classified information briefly went down. The agency said the problem occurred during scheduled routine maintenance and that its mission-critical capabilities remained fully operational.
A PHP flaw and systems that did not restart

Fox Business reported that Clayton linked the outages to patching that followed a vulnerability in PHP, the widely used web programming language. He described systems that are taken offline, upgraded and then fail to hand off to other systems as they should. He said the FBI and the NSA had told operators to take vulnerable systems down and install the fix, and he said more patches would follow as government infrastructure is upgraded.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the failures were unrelated to one another and not tied to a hostile country, calling them unsettling but attributing them to ordinary computer errors with different causes, according to ABC News. Fox Business separately quoted Rubio saying officials had found no evidence that hackers, criminal groups or foreign governments were responsible.

Sen. Mark Warner of Virginia, vice chairman of the Senate Intelligence Committee, said there was no indication the incidents were the result of a cyberattack and that the evidence points toward legitimate efforts to secure systems. He added that AI makes it possible to identify vulnerabilities across enormous numbers of systems at unprecedented speed, creating pressure on companies and agencies to patch immediately and often all at once, according to ABC News. Clayton also said AI can scan systems more quickly, which has increased the ability to find vulnerabilities.

Clayton also called for continued cooperation between the government and AI companies, so that cyber issues are dealt with before each new generation of frontier models is released, Fox Business reported.
The FAA ground stop had a different cause

Not every recent failure fits the patching explanation. The Federal Aviation Administration ordered a nationwide ground stop on November 13 after a communications problem affecting air traffic control, forcing airlines to delay and cancel thousands of flights. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the trouble began when an L3Harris contractor, switching lines from copper to fiber at a remote FAA site, triggered a flood of more than 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds on routers, Fortune reported. Duffy said it was not a foreign actor.

Some outside experts remain cautious. Ram Dantu, founding director of the University of North Texas Center for Cyber and AI Security, told Fox News that nobody can guarantee the outages were not a cyberattack and said daytime upgrades are unusual because engineers normally schedule them overnight and in stages.

The officials' account shifts the worry from attackers to defenders. If AI tools surface serious flaws faster than organizations can safely test fixes, the rush to patch can itself knock systems offline, and critical services may face a choice between running exposed software and risking an unplanned outage.
Clayton said more patches are coming as government infrastructure is upgraded, so the next test is whether agencies and banks can stage those fixes without new outages.
